analysis_scope.sampling_notes: The checkout was supplied as a shallow clone with depth 50, so history beyond that boundary may be unavailable. The repository exposes only two commits, and git reports the checkout as non-shallow, suggesting the visible history may nevertheless be complete. All 15 tracked files were inventoried; the conversion script was read fully, CSV inspection was limited to headers and line counts, and the approximately 163 MB of Parquet data was sampled only through file metadata.

observed_capabilities.statement: The repository contains a Python script that reads nine weekly tracking CSV files with PyArrow and writes one Parquet file for each week.
It stores four tabular NFL datasets covering games, players, plays, and tackle outcomes, along with nine weekly tracking datasets in Apache Parquet format.
The gameId, playId, and nflId fields provide apparent join keys across the game, play, tackle, player, and tracking data needed to investigate tackling events.

architecture.statement: The implemented pipeline is a single, linear preprocessing script with nine repeated CSV-read and Parquet-write operations; there are no modules, services, databases, or downstream analysis components.
Input locations are nine absolute, machine-specific filesystem paths, while outputs are written as week1.parquet through week9.parquet in the current working directory.
The repository functions primarily as a checked-in data snapshot and conversion utility rather than a completed NFL tackling analysis application.

accomplishments.statement: Nine generated Apache Parquet files are tracked, providing artifact evidence that the weekly conversion workflow was completed at least once.
The repository assembles 136 game rows, 1,683 player rows, 12,486 play rows, and 17,426 tackle rows, based on CSV line counts excluding headers.
The supplied data schemas include tackle, assist, forced-fumble, and missed-tackle indicators alongside play context and player metadata.

gaps.statement: No code performs statistical analysis, modeling, visualization, evaluation, or reporting of NFL tackling behavior.
The conversion script is not portable because every source path is hard-coded to one user's local desktop hierarchy.
There is no dependency manifest, setup guidance, command-line interface, input validation, error handling, test suite, or CI workflow supporting reproducible execution.
The plaintext file named test contains only the word 'test' and does not constitute executable verification.
No README, license, data dictionary, or source attribution explains the intended analysis, dataset origin, permitted redistribution, or field semantics.

risks.statement: A fresh user cannot reproduce the conversion without reconstructing the missing source-file locations and independently identifying and installing compatible PyArrow dependencies.
Tracking approximately 163 MB of generated Parquet binaries directly in Git produces a roughly 145 MB object pack and can make cloning and future data revisions costly.
Public redistribution and reuse obligations cannot be assessed because the checked-in datasets have no documented provenance or license.
The repository name implies a completed analysis, while the tracked implementation stops at data conversion and storage.

suggested_next_actions.statement: Document the repository's intended outcome, dataset provenance and license, field relationships, setup requirements, and current limitation to preprocessing.
Replace the repeated absolute paths with configurable input and output directories, iterate over week numbers, remove unused imports, and pin the required Python dependencies.
Add a small reproducibility check that validates expected schemas and row counts without requiring the full dataset.

Decide whether to add the intended tackling analysis or preserve this as an archived data-preparation snapshot, and consider external artifact storage or Git LFS if the generated Parquet files must remain available.

questions: Was this repository intended for a course project, competition submission, or reusable NFL analysis?
What is the authoritative source and redistribution license for the checked-in data?
Does the actual tackling analysis exist in another repository, notebook, or untracked local file?
Are the nine Parquet snapshots still useful enough to retain, or can they be regenerated or archived elsewhere?

evidence.summary: Public repository on main with no description, no open issues or pull requests, and a last recorded push on 2023-11-21.
The complete tracked tree contains 15 files: one Python script, four CSV datasets, nine Parquet datasets, and one five-byte plaintext placeholder.
A 50-line script imports Pandas and PyArrow, defines nine absolute weekly CSV paths, and performs nine explicit PyArrow CSV-to-Parquet conversions; Pandas and datetime are unused.
CSV headers expose game, player, play, and tackle schemas. The files contain 137, 1,684, 12,487, and 17,427 lines respectively, including one header line each.
Nine tracked files are recognized as Apache Parquet and range from approximately 15.3 MB to 19.7 MB, totaling approximately 163 MB.
A five-byte plaintext file contains only the word 'test' and has no executable test behavior.
No README, documentation, dependency manifest, license, automated test, CI workflow, notebook, demo, credential-named file, or analysis/report artifact is tracked.

The visible history has two commits, both dated 2023-11-21: an initial placeholder commit and a DataConversion commit that added the script and all datasets. No tags or additional branches are present.

confidence.rationale: The complete small source tree, CSV schemas, generated-file metadata, and visible history clearly establish that the repository contains a one-step data-conversion prototype rather than an implemented analysis. Confidence is limited by the absence of stated purpose, provenance, tests, execution evidence, and inspectable Parquet metadata.

limitations: The supplied checkout was described as depth 50, so older history would not be visible if more than 50 commits existed, although only two commits are exposed and Git reports the checkout as non-shallow.
The conversion was not executed because analysis was read-only, source CSV paths are machine-specific, and PyArrow is not installed in the environment.
Parquet contents and schemas were not inspected; conclusions about their role rely on file metadata, filenames, the conversion script, and the tracked commit.
No owner-supplied context establishes whether the repository remains useful, whether analysis exists elsewhere, or whether the data may be redistributed.
Lifecycle, priority, and storage changes remain suggestions requiring owner review.
